title: Thermal & Structural Analysis
description: Analysis planning, loads and boundary conditions, FEA modeling, results interpretation, structural, dynamics, thermal, thermal expansion, pressure, battery and analysis documentation.

items.text: A list of parts and load cases that need analysis is agreed at the start of detailed design
items.hint: Base it on the requirements, risk analysis and past failures. Unanalyzed critical parts are usually found during testing, when changes are expensive.

items.text: Acceptance criteria and safety factors are defined before any analysis is run
items.hint: State the allowable (yield, ultimate, strain, temperature, deflection) and safety factor for each load case in the plan. Criteria chosen after seeing results invite wishful thinking.

items.text: Hand calculations bound each critical result before or alongside FEA
items.hint: Beam, plate, pressure-vessel or thermal resistance hand calcs catch unit errors and wrong boundary conditions. Large disagreement with FEA needs an explanation.

items.text: Rules of thumb used in place of analysis are labeled as such and recorded with their source
items.hint: Mark them clearly in the design record so reviewers know which numbers were not calculated.

items.text: The analysis type (static, modal, transient, nonlinear, thermal, CFD) matches the physics of each load case
items.hint: Impact and snap fits are not linear static problems. Large deflections, contact and yielding need nonlinear analysis.

items.text: Analysis results feed back into a decision: design change, test or accepted risk
items.hint: Every result should close with an action. Reports that conclude nothing waste the effort.

items.text: Analysis schedule allows results before tooling release
items.hint: Tie analysis milestones to the tooling kickoff. Results after tool steel is cut become a recut.

items.text: The software, version and solver settings used are recorded
items.hint: Results can change between versions and solver settings. Record them for reproducibility.

items.text: Load cases are derived from the requirements, including normal use, reasonably foreseeable misuse and abuse
items.hint: Trace each load case to a requirement or risk item. Sitting, stepping, dropping and lifting by the wrong feature are common misuse loads.

items.text: Drop and impact loads are included for handheld and portable products
items.hint: Define the drop height, surface and orientations from the requirement. Use the results to rank risk, not as a pass/fail replacement for testing.

items.text: Transport and packaging loads (vibration, stacking, shock) are included
items.hint: Use the shipping test standard named in the requirements to define the loads. Stacking compression on packaged products can exceed use loads.

items.text: Assembly loads such as screw torque, press fits, heat staking and insertion forces are included
items.hint: Boss splitting and stripped threads often come from assembly, not use. Apply the bolt preload or interference as a load case.

items.text: Fastener preload is modeled where it affects joint stiffness, contact or separation
items.hint: Use bolt pretension features in the solver, with preload from torque per the fastener supplier's torque-tension data.

items.text: Boundary conditions represent the real supports and do not overconstrain the model
items.hint: Fixed faces add artificial stiffness and stress. Use the actual mounting features, springs or remote supports, and check reaction forces.

items.text: Bonded versus contact interfaces are chosen deliberately and justified in the report
items.hint: Bonded contact transfers tension through faces that would separate in reality. Use frictional or frictionless contact where parts can slide or open.

items.text: Reaction forces sum to the applied loads
items.hint: Check the reaction-force probe in the solver. A mismatch reveals missing loads, wrong units or rigid body motion.

items.text: Load magnitude and direction worst cases are identified, not just one nominal load
items.hint: Sweep directions where the load can come from different angles. The worst case is often off-axis.

items.text: Loads from internal components (battery, motors, heat sinks, displays) are applied with their masses
items.hint: Heavy internal parts load their mounts during drop and vibration. Use point masses with correct center of gravity location.

items.text: Geometry defeaturing (removed fillets, holes, ribs) is listed and justified as not affecting the results
items.hint: Removing a fillet at a high-stress location changes the answer. Keep features in the region of interest.

items.text: A mesh convergence study is done at the locations used for decisions
items.hint: Refine the mesh until peak stress or displacement changes less than a stated tolerance. Report the convergence plot or table.

items.text: Element type and order suit the geometry (e.g. second-order tetrahedra, shells for thin sheet metal)
items.hint: First-order tetrahedra are too stiff in bending. Use at least two to three elements through thin walls, or shells.

items.text: The material model (linear elastic, elastic-plastic, hyperelastic) matches the expected behavior
items.hint: Linear elastic results above yield are meaningless. Use plasticity for yielding metals and hyperelastic models for elastomers.

items.text: Glass-filled plastic parts account for fiber orientation and anisotropy, or use conservative properties
items.hint: Map fiber orientation from mold flow into the FEA where results are critical, otherwise use the transverse (lower) properties and weld line knockdowns.

items.text: Material data used is at the operating temperature and, where relevant, conditioned moisture state
items.hint: Enter temperature-dependent properties from the supplier for the analyzed temperature. Room-temperature data overstates plastic strength at elevated temperature.

items.text: Stress singularities at sharp corners, point loads and constraints are identified and not used as design stresses
items.hint: Stress that keeps rising with mesh refinement is a singularity. Add the real fillet, or evaluate stress away from the singular point.

items.text: Units are consistent throughout the model and inputs
items.hint: Check density, modulus and load units against the solver unit system. Unit errors are among the most common FEA mistakes.

items.text: Symmetry, if used, is valid for geometry, loads and constraints
items.hint: Symmetric models miss asymmetric buckling and vibration modes. Check that loads are truly symmetric.

items.text: Material properties assigned to every body match the specified grade on the BOM
items.hint: Check each body's material assignment in the model tree. Default steel on a plastic part is a frequent mistake.

items.text: Peak stresses are compared with the allowable for the material and failure mode, with the agreed safety factor
items.hint: Use von Mises for ductile metals and principal stress or strain for brittle materials and plastics. Report the margin explicitly.

items.text: Displacements are checked against functional limits such as clearances, alignments and seal compression
items.hint: Overlay deformed shape with nearby parts. Excess deflection can cause rubbing, gaps or loss of sealing even without failure.

items.text: Buckling is checked for slender or thin-walled parts under compression
items.hint: Run a linear buckling analysis and apply a knockdown for imperfections, or a nonlinear analysis for critical cases.

items.text: Fatigue life is evaluated for cyclically loaded parts using an S-N curve for the material and the expected cycle count
items.hint: Use the cycle count from the life requirement and include mean stress effects. Plastics fatigue at lower stress than static strength suggests.

items.text: Creep and stress relaxation are evaluated for plastic parts under sustained load
items.hint: Use creep modulus or isochronous curves for the load duration and temperature. Bosses, clips and press fits loosen over time.

items.text: Snap fit strain at full deflection is below the allowable for the material grade
items.hint: Compute the peak strain during assembly (not just the latched state) and compare against the supplier's allowable strain for the number of cycles.

items.text: Results are plotted with a sensible scale and the deformed shape is reviewed for plausibility
items.hint: Check exaggerated deformed shape and animation. Parts flying apart or moving through each other point to modeling errors.

items.text: A second engineer reviews the model setup and results before they are used for decisions
items.hint: The reviewer checks loads, boundary conditions, materials and mesh, not just the final plot.

items.text: The model is correlated with a physical test or a known reference case where results drive critical decisions
items.hint: Compare strain gauge, deflection or temperature measurements with prediction, and update the model if it disagrees.

items.text: Sensitivity to uncertain inputs (friction, material properties, contact stiffness) is checked
items.hint: Run the analysis at both ends of the input range. Conclusions that flip with a reasonable input change need a test.

items.text: Failure modes are reported with location and the design change that addresses them
items.hint: Name the feature and propose the fix. A plot without a conclusion leaves the designer guessing.

items.text: Load paths from the point of load application to the supports are identified and continuous
items.hint: Sketch the load path and check every joint, weld and fastener along it. Gaps in the path usually show up as unexpected deformation.

items.text: Fastener and joint loads (tension, shear, prying) are calculated and below the rated capacity
items.hint: Extract forces at each fastener from FEA or calculate by hand. Include prying action and thread strip in the base material.

items.text: Weld strength is checked with the weld size, process and reduced heat-affected-zone properties
items.hint: Weld toes are fatigue hotspots. Use the structural welding standard named in the requirements for allowables.

items.text: Factor of safety follows the applicable standard or requirement and is documented for each load case
items.hint: Name the source of each factor. Lifting, pressure and overhead equipment often have prescribed factors.

items.text: The predicted failure mode is safe: it gives warning, fails gradually or fails in a direction that does not harm people
items.hint: Prefer yielding before fracture. Check that a failed part does not release stored energy or drop loads on users.

items.text: Load ratings marked on the product or in the manual are supported by the analysis with the required margin
items.hint: Cross-check the rated load in labeling against the analyzed and tested capacity.

items.text: Natural frequencies are calculated and separated from known excitation frequencies
items.hint: Run a modal analysis and compare against motor, fan, pump and transport vibration frequencies. Rule of thumb: keep a clear margin between the first mode and the main excitation.

items.text: Random or sine vibration response is evaluated for the transport or operating vibration profile
items.hint: Use the profile from the requirements and include appropriate damping. Check PCB and heavy-component mounts.

items.text: Shock loads are evaluated for the specified shock pulse
items.hint: Use transient or response-spectrum analysis. Check mounts of heavy components and brittle parts like displays and glass.

items.text: Drop simulation assumptions (impact surface, contact, material strain-rate effects) are stated and its limits are acknowledged
items.hint: Explicit drop simulations are sensitive to material data and contact. Use them to compare designs and find weak points, and confirm with physical drop tests.

items.text: Moving masses and mechanisms are checked for dynamic loads, including end-of-travel impact
items.hint: End stops, latches and hinges see peak loads at impact. Include velocity and stop stiffness.

items.text: Damping values used in dynamic analyses are justified by data or conservative assumptions
items.hint: Response at resonance is very sensitive to damping. State the value and the source.

items.text: Heat sources and their power dissipation come from the EE power budget, including worst-case operating modes
items.hint: Use the current power budget for every component, including peak and sustained modes. Analysis with stale or guessed power is not useful.

items.text: Maximum ambient temperature for analysis is the worst case from the requirements, including enclosure placement
items.hint: Consider installation in cabinets, near other equipment, in vehicles or in direct sun. Ambient inside the installation can be well above room ambient.

items.text: Conduction paths from hot components to the enclosure or heat sink are identified and modeled
items.hint: Check every interface along the path. A path through a thin plastic wall or an air gap is often the bottleneck.

items.text: Thermal interface materials are specified with thickness, compression and thermal resistance at that compression
items.hint: Thermal pad resistance depends on compression. Check the gap stack-up gives the intended compression without overloading components or the PCB.

items.text: Natural or forced convection assumptions are stated, including the orientation of the product
items.hint: Natural convection depends strongly on orientation and vent placement. Analyze the worst installed orientation.

items.text: Fan selection is based on the system impedance curve intersecting the fan curve, with margin
items.hint: Estimate system pressure drop from CFD or hand calcs, including filters and grilles. Account for filter clogging and fan aging.

items.text: CFD assumptions (turbulence model, mesh, boundary conditions, radiation) are documented and checked for sensitivity
items.hint: Check mesh independence at component temperatures. Include radiation where natural convection dominates.

items.text: Every component temperature is below its rated limit with a margin agreed with the EE
items.hint: Compare predicted junction or case temperatures with datasheet limits and derating rules from the EE.

items.text: Touch temperatures of accessible surfaces are within the limits of the applicable safety standard
items.hint: Identify which surfaces are touchable and for how long, and check against the standard's surface temperature limits for that material and contact duration.

items.text: Solar loading is included for outdoor products
items.hint: Apply solar flux from the requirement or design climate data, with surface absorptivity for the actual color and finish.

items.text: Plastic parts near heat sources stay below their long-term temperature limits
items.hint: Check predicted part temperatures against RTI or HDT with margin. Hot spots near power components and LEDs soften bosses and clips.

items.text: Battery cell temperatures stay within the cell manufacturer's limits for charge and discharge
items.hint: Charge limits are usually tighter than discharge limits. Coordinate with the EE on charge rate at high ambient.

items.text: Vent and filter placement does not short-circuit airflow from outlet back to inlet
items.hint: Check CFD streamlines or smoke tests. Recirculation raises inlet temperature and defeats the cooling design.

items.text: Transient thermal behavior is evaluated where duty cycles or startup peaks matter
items.hint: Short bursts may be acceptable even if steady-state would not be. Use the duty cycle from the requirements.

items.text: Condensation risk is evaluated for products that cycle through the dew point
items.hint: Cold surfaces inside a warm humid enclosure collect water. Check temperature cycling and venting strategy with the enclosure review.

items.text: CTE mismatch between joined parts is evaluated over the full temperature range
items.hint: Long plastic parts on metal frames, glass in housings and overmolds are common problem areas. Calculate differential growth by hand over the part length.

items.text: Thermal stresses from constrained expansion are below allowables at temperature extremes
items.hint: Run a thermal-structural analysis or hand calc for bonded, press-fit or fastened dissimilar materials.

items.text: Clearances and fits remain functional at both temperature extremes
items.hint: Recompute critical gaps at hot and cold. Coordinate with the tolerance stack-ups in the tolerancing review.

items.text: Slotted holes, floating mounts or compliant features allow thermal growth where needed
items.hint: Check that only one fixed point exists along a long part. Over-constrained long parts buckle or crack.

items.text: Pressure-containing parts are analyzed for the maximum operating pressure with the required margin
items.hint: Include pressure spikes from valves closing or pumps starting. Use the rated pressure from the requirements.

items.text: Burst pressure factor meets the applicable standard or requirement
items.hint: State the required burst factor and its source, and check the analysis and planned test against it.

items.text: Pressure-induced deformation does not open leak paths at seals and joints
items.hint: Check the seal compression at peak pressure in the deformed model. Housings bulge and unload O-rings.

items.text: Pressure drop and flow through the fluid path meet requirements
items.hint: Use hand calcs or CFD for the full path, including fittings, filters and valves.

items.text: Plastic pressure parts are evaluated for long-term creep rupture at temperature
items.hint: Use long-term hydrostatic strength data from the supplier. Short-term burst tests do not predict long-term failure.

items.text: Thermal runaway propagation between cells is considered and the mitigation strategy is agreed with the EE
items.hint: Review cell spacing, barriers and venting paths. Coordinate with the battery safety standard named in the requirements.

items.text: Cell venting gases have a path out of the enclosure that does not direct them at the user
items.hint: Check vent direction and enclosure pressure relief. A sealed enclosure can rupture during a cell vent event.

items.text: Cell swelling over life and mounting pressure are within the cell manufacturer's limits
items.hint: Allow space for end-of-life swelling per the cell datasheet. Check the mounting design does not apply point loads to cells.

items.text: Cells are protected from puncture and crush by the enclosure and internal structure under drop and impact loads
items.hint: Check the drop and crush analysis results at the cell envelope, including sharp internal features such as screw tips, ribs and PCB components near the cells.

items.text: Each analysis has a report with inputs, assumptions, load cases, results and conclusions
items.hint: A reviewer should be able to repeat the analysis from the report alone.

items.text: The report states the CAD revision and part numbers analyzed
items.hint: Results on an old revision may no longer apply. Re-run or justify when the geometry changes.

items.text: Analysis files (model, mesh, results) are archived with the project
items.hint: Store native files in the project repository with the CAD revision. Lost models mean rerunning from scratch.

items.text: Assumptions and simplifications are listed with their expected effect on the results
items.hint: Mark which assumptions are conservative and which are not.

items.text: Open issues and recommendations from analysis are tracked to closure
items.hint: Enter them in the issue tracker or design review action list with an owner.

items.text: Analysis results that support certification or regulatory submissions are under document control
items.hint: Release the report with a document number and revision so it can be referenced in the technical file.
